QuestionStmt.S: The solution of $(1 + y^2) + \left( x - e^{\tan^{-1}y} \right) \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ is

Option1Stmt.S: $2xe^{\tan^{-1}y} = e^{2\tan^{-1}y} + k$, where $k$ is the constant of integration

Option2Stmt.S: $x \cdot e^{\tan^{-1}y} = e^{\tan^{-1}y} + k$, where $k$ is the constant of integration

Option3Stmt.S: $x \cdot e^{2\tan^{-1}y} = e^{\tan^{-1}y} + k$, where $k$ is the constant of integration

Option4Stmt.S: $x = 2 + k \cdot e^{-\tan^{-1}y}$, where $k$ is the constant of integration

Solution.S:
$$(1 + y^2) + \left( x - e^{\tan^{-1}y} \right) \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{dx}{dy} + \frac{x}{1 + y^2} = \frac{e^{\tan^{-1}y}}{1 + y^2}$$

$$\therefore \text{I.F.} = e^{\int \frac{1}{1 + y^2} dy} = e^{\tan^{-1}y}$$

$$\therefore \text{Solution of the given equation is}$$

$$x \cdot e^{\tan^{-1}y} = \int \frac{e^{\tan^{-1}y}}{1 + y^2} \cdot e^{\tan^{-1}y} \, dy + k$$

$$\Rightarrow xe^{\tan^{-1}y} = \int t \, dt + k \quad \therefore \left[ \text{Put } e^{\tan^{-1}y} = t \right]$$

$$\Rightarrow xe^{\tan^{-1}y} = \frac{t^2}{2} + k$$

$$\Rightarrow xe^{\tan^{-1}y} = \frac{\left( e^{\tan^{-1}y} \right)^2}{2} + k$$

$$\Rightarrow 2xe^{\tan^{-1}y} = e^{2\tan^{-1}y} + k$$
